title: Vector Spaces and Dimensions
content: Vector Spaces and Dimensions In this chapter, we introduce the fundamental concept of a vector space and discuss its properties, including basis and dimension.

title: 1.1 Vector Spaces
content:
Vector Spaces Why do we bother with a list of eight axioms? To a student first encountering Linear Algebra, this can feel like a bureaucratic exercise in “checking boxes.” However, there is a profound beauty hidden in this formality. In our preliminary chapter, we saw three very different worlds: the world of geometric arrows (
R^n), the world of functions (F[x]), and the world of matrices (M_{m 	imes n}). On the surface, an arrow is not a polynomial, and a polynomial is not a matrix. But if you squint, they all behave the same: you can add them, and you can scale them. By defining a Vector Space through these axioms, we are choosing to ignore what the objects are and focus entirely on how they act. If we prove a theorem using only these eight axioms, that theorem becomes a “universal law” that applies to arrows, functions, and matrices all at once. This is the power of abstraction: solve the problem once, and you solve it for every universe that obeys these rules. Vector Spaces and Vectors [Vector Space] A set V over a field F with two operations: addition + and scalar multiplication \cdot + : V 	imes V 	o V, \quad \cdot : F 	imes V 	o V such that satisfy the following axioms for all \v_1, \v_2, \v_3 \in V and \alpha,  eta \in F: 1. \v_1 + \v_2 = \v_2 + \v_1 2. (\v_1 + \v_2) + \v_3 = \v_1 + (\v_2 + \v_3) 3. There exists \mathbf{0} \in V such that \v_1 + \mathbf{0} = \v_1 4. There exists \v_1' \in V such that \v_1 + \v_1' = \mathbf{0} 5. \alpha(\v_1 + \v_2) = \alpha\v_1 + \alpha\v_2 6. (\alpha+ eta)\v_1 = \alpha\v_1 +  eta\v_1 7. \alpha( eta\v_1) = (\alpha eta)\v_1 8. 1\v_1 = \v_1 Instead of writing (V, +, \cdot) is a vector space over F, we usually simplify it to V is a vector space over F, or even just V is a vector space if the context is clear. We sometimes will abuse the name and refer to \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}_V \in V as the “zero vector” of the vector space V. Readers should not confuse \mathbf{0}_V with the zero scalar 0 = 0_F \in F from the field F. [Examples of Vector Spaces] The following are classic examples of vector spaces: 1. The standard example: F^n with the usual operations of + and \cdot is a vector space over F. 2. Working with polynomials is common too: F[x] with the usual operations of + and \cdot is a vector space over F. 3. Let \sD be any open interval. Let C(\sD) \coloneqq \left\{ f: \sD 	o 
R: f 	ext{ is continuous} ight\}. Then C(\sD) is a vector space over 
R. The zero vector of this vector space is given by the zero function (x \mapsto 0). 4. Let F be any field and fix n \in 
N. Then M_n(F) is a vector space over F. 5. The set V = \mathbb{R}_{>0} of positive real numbers forms a vector space over F = \mathbb{R} under the following operations: for x, y \in V and \alpha \in F, define x \oplus y \coloneqq xy, \quad \alpha \odot x \coloneqq x^\alpha = e^{\alpha \log x}. Under these operations, the zero vector is \mathbf{0} = 1, and the additive inverse of x is x^{-1}. You can check if addition and scalar multiplication make sense and follow all axioms of vector spaces. [
Q Adjoin \sqrt{2}] Show that 
Q(\sqrt{2}) \coloneqq \left\{ a + b \sqrt{2} : a, b \in 
Q ight\} is a vector space over 
Q by checking all eight axioms. Let \v_1 = a_1 + b_1\sqrt{2}, \v_2 = a_2 + b_2\sqrt{2}, \v_3 = a_3 + b_3\sqrt{2} \in 
Q(\sqrt{2}) and \alpha,  eta \in 
Q. 1. 2. 3. The element \mathbf{0} = 0 + 0\sqrt{2} = 0 \in 
Q(\sqrt{2}) satisfies 4. For \v_1 = a_1 + b_1\sqrt{2}, define -\v_1 \coloneqq (-a_1) + (-b_1)\sqrt{2} \in 
Q(\sqrt{2}). Then 5. 6. 7. 8. Thus 
Q(\sqrt{2}) is a vector space over 
Q. [Vectors and Scalars] Let V be a vector space over F. Then the elements of V are called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars. Additionally, \mathbf{0} \in V is called the zero vector, and (\v_1') in (VS4) is called the inverse element of \v_1. Vector Space Theorems [Left Cancellation Law] Let V be a vector space over F, let \u, \v_1, \v_2 \in V. If \u + \v_1 = \u + \v_2, then \v_1 = \v_2. Let \u' be an inverse of \u. [Right Cancellation Law] Let V be a vector space over F, let \u, \v_1, \v_2 \in V. If \v_1 + \u = \v_2 + \u, then \v_1 = \v_2. Since we have \u + \v_1 = \u + \v_2 \implies \v_1 = \v_2, applying (VS1) to it gives \v_1 + \u = \v_2 + \u \implies \v_1 = \v_2. [Zero Vector is Unique] Let V be a vector space over F. The zero vector \mathbf{0} \in V is unique. Suppose that there are two vectors \mathbf{0}_1, \mathbf{0}_2. [Additive Inverse is Unique] Let V be a vector space over F. Then for every \v \in V, its additive inverse described in (VS4), which is \v', is unique. Let \v_1', \v_2' both be inverses of \v. Then [Notation of Additive Inverse] The unique inverse of a vector \v \in V, for a vector space V over F, will be denoted as -\v. [Zero Scalar Annihilates] Let \v \in V for a vector space V over F. Then 0 \cdot \v = \mathbf{0}. Let \w = 0 \cdot \v. We show that \w = \mathbf{0}. [Negation as Scalar Multiplication] Let V be a vector space over F and \v \in V be any vector. Then -\v = (-1) \cdot \v. We show that (-1) \cdot \v is an additive inverse of \v: By (*), we use @thm-zero-scalar-mult. Since (-1) \cdot \v is an additive inverse of \v, by uniqueness we have -\v = (-1) \cdot \v. [Negative Scalar Distribution] Let V be a vector space over F. For any \alpha \in F and \v \in V, we have (-\alpha)\v = -(\alpha\v). We show that (-\alpha)\v is an additive inverse of \alpha\v: By (*), we use @thm-zero-scalar-mult. Since (-\alpha)\v is an additive inverse of \alpha\v, by uniqueness we have (-\alpha)\v = -(\alpha\v). [Scalar Multiplication by Zero Vector] Let V be a vector space over F. For any scalar \alpha \in F, we have \alpha\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}. Let \w = \alpha\mathbf{0}. We show that \w = \mathbf{0}. [Zero Product Law] Let V be a vector space over F, \v \in V, and \alpha \in F. If \alpha\v = \mathbf{0}, then either \alpha = 0 or \v = \mathbf{0}. Suppose \alpha\v = \mathbf{0}. We consider two cases: - Case \alpha = 0: Then the statement holds. - Case \alpha 
eq 0: Since F is a field, \alpha has a multiplicative inverse \alpha^{-1}. Thus, if \alpha 
eq 0, we must have \v = \mathbf{0}.

title: 1.2 Subspaces
content:
Subspaces Some vector spaces might be “too big” and be unwieldy to deal with. Therefore, it is often convenient to look at “smaller vector spaces” inside a given vector space. These are called subspaces. Definition and the Subspace Test [Subspace] Let V be a vector space over F. A subset W of V is called a subspace of V, if W is also a vector space over F with addition and scalar multiplication inherited from V. Let (V, +, \cdot) be a vector space over F, and W \subseteq V. If (W, +, \cdot) is also a vector space over F then W is a subspace of V. [Trivial Subspaces] Given a vector space V, then - V is a subspace of V itself; - \left\{ \mathbf{0} ight\} is a subspace of V (also known as the “zero subspace”); - \varnothing is not a subspace of V. [Subspace Test] Let V be a vector space over F and W \subseteq V. Then W is a subspace of V if and only if the following are satisfied: - W is non-empty; - W is closed under addition: \w_1 + \w_2 \in W for all \w_1, \w_2 \in W; - W is closed under scalar multiplication: \alpha \w \in W for all \alpha \in F and \w \in W. (\Rightarrow) If W is a subspace, then W is a vector space, so it contains the zero vector (hence non-empty) and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication by definition. (\Leftarrow) Assume the three conditions hold. Since W \subseteq V, the operations on W are inherited from V, so associativity, commutativity, and distributivity are automatically satisfied. It remains to verify the existence of identity elements and inverses. - Zero vector: Since W 
eq \varnothing, there exists \w \in W. By closure under scalar multiplication, 0 \cdot \w = \mathbf{0} \in W. - Additive inverse: For any \w \in W, closure under scalar multiplication gives (-1) \cdot \w = -\w \in W. Thus W is a vector space under the inherited operations, i.e., a subspace of V. Note that from the proof, the first condition of the Subspace Test can be replaced by the requirement that W contains the zero vector of V. In practice, to test whether a given subset of a vector space is a subspace, we use @thm-subspace-test instead of checking all eight vector space axioms from scratch, which is much less tedious. Moreover, some introductory textbooks use @thm-subspace-test as the definition of a subspace. While this is logically equivalent, it can be somewhat less intuitive than defining a subspace as a subset that is itself a vector space. Examples of Subspaces [Line as Subspace] W = \left\{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : x + 2y = 0 ight\} is a subspace of 
R^2. Indeed: - Zero vector: (0, 0) \in W since 0 + 2(0) = 0. - Addition: If (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2) \in W, then (x_1+x_2) + 2(y_1+y_2) = (x_1+2y_1) + (x_2+2y_2) = 0 + 0 = 0, so their sum is in W. - Scalar multiplication: If (x, y) \in W and c \in 
R, then (cx) + 2(cy) = c(x+2y) = c(0) = 0, so c(x, y) \in W. [Translated Line is Not a Subspace] W = \left\{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : x + 2y = 3 ight\} is not a subspace of 
R^2. This is because it does not contain the zero vector: 0 + 2(0) = 0 
eq 3, so (0, 0) 
otin W. [Polynomials of Bounded Degree] Let F[x] be the vector space of all polynomials over a field F. For a fixed n \in 
N, the set F[x]_{\leq n} of polynomials of degree at most n is a subspace of F[x]. - Zero vector: The zero polynomial has degree -\infty, so 0 \in F[x]_{\leq n}. - Addition: If \deg p \leq n and \deg q \leq n, then \deg(p+q) \leq \max(\deg p, \deg q) \leq n. - Scalar multiplication: If \deg p \leq n and c \in F, then \deg(cp) \leq \deg p \leq n. [Polynomials of Exact Degree] The set F[x]_{=n} of polynomials of degree exactly n is not a subspace of F[x]. - It does not contain the zero vector (since \deg 0 = -\infty 
eq n). - It is not closed under addition. For example, if p(x) = x^n + x and q(x) = -x^n, both have degree n, but p(x) + q(x) = x, which has degree 1 
eq n (assuming n > 1). [Differentiable Functions] Let C(
R) = \{f : 
R 	o 
R \mid f 	ext{ is continuous}\} be the set of all continuous functions on 
R. We consider the set of differentiable functions: D(
R) = \{ f : 
R 	o 
R \mid f 	ext{ is differentiable} \} To verify that D(
R) is a subspace of C(
R): - Subset: Since differentiability implies continuity, we have D(
R) \subseteq C(
R). - Zero vector: The zero function f(x) = 0 is differentiable, so \mathbf{0} \in D(
R). - Closure under addition: If f, g \in D(
R), then f+g is differentiable with (f+g)' = f' + g', so f+g \in D(
R). - Closure under scalar multiplication: If f \in D(
R) and c \in 
R, then cf is differentiable with (cf)' = c f', so cf \in D(
R). Thus, D(
R) is a subspace of C(
R). [Symmetric Matrices] The set of all symmetric matrices in M_n(F), denoted by S_n(F) = \{ \A \in M_n(F) : \A = \A^{	op} \}, is a subspace of M_n(F). - Zero vector: The zero matrix \O is symmetric since \O^{	op} = \O, so \O \in S_n(F). - Addition: If \A, \B \in S_n(F), then (\A+\B)^{	op} = \A^{	op} + \B^{	op} = \A + \B, so \A+\B \in S_n(F). - Scalar multiplication: If \A \in S_n(F) and c \in F, then (c\A)^{	op} = c\A^{	op} = c\A, so c\A \in S_n(F). [Trace-free Matrices] The set of all trace-free matrices in M_n(F), denoted by W = \{ \A \in M_n(F) : 	r(\A) = 0 \}, is a subspace of M_n(F). - Zero vector: 	r(\O) = 0 + 0 + \cdots + 0 = 0, so \O \in W. - Addition: If \A, \B \in W, then 	r(\A+\B) = 	r(\A) + 	r(\B) = 0 + 0 = 0, so \A+\B \in W. - Scalar multiplication: If \A \in W and c \in F, then 	r(c\A) = c 	r(\A) = c(0) = 0, so c\A \in W. Intersections and Unions [Intersection of Subspaces] Let W_1 and W_2 be subspaces of a vector space V. Then the intersection W_1 \cap W_2 is also a subspace of V. We use the Subspace Test (@thm-subspace-test) on W = W_1 \cap W_2: - Zero vector: Since W_1 and W_2 are subspaces, \mathbf{0} \in W_1 and \mathbf{0} \in W_2. Thus \mathbf{0} \in W_1 \cap W_2. - Closure under addition: Let \w, \z \in W_1 \cap W_2. Then \w, \z \in W_1 and \w, \z \in W_2. Since W_1 and W_2 are subspaces, they are closed under addition, so \w + \z \in W_1 and \w + \z \in W_2. Hence \w + \z \in W_1 \cap W_2. - Closure under scalar multiplication: Let \w \in W_1 \cap W_2 and c \in F. Then \w \in W_1 and \w \in W_2. Since W_1 and W_2 are closed under scalar multiplication, c\w \in W_1 and c\w \in W_2. Hence c\w \in W_1 \cap W_2. Since all three conditions of the Subspace Test are satisfied, W_1 \cap W_2 is a subspace of V. Unlike the intersection, the union of two subspaces is not necessarily a subspace. For W_1 \cup W_2 to be a subspace, one subspace must be contained within the other (i.e., W_1 \subseteq W_2 or W_2 \subseteq W_1). [Union of Axes] Consider the vector space V = 
R^2. Let W_1 be the x-axis and W_2 be the y-axis: W_1 = \{ (x, 0) : x \in 
R \}, \quad W_2 = \{ (0, y) : y \in 
R \}. Both W_1 and W_2 are subspaces of 
R^2. However, their union W_1 \cup W_2 is not a subspace because it is not closed under addition. Indeed, (1, 0) \in W_1 \subseteq W_1 \cup W_2 and (0, 1) \in W_2 \subseteq W_1 \cup W_2, but their sum: (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) is not in W_1 \cup W_2 since (1, 1) is neither on the x-axis nor the y-axis. [Union of Subspaces] Let W_1, W_2 be subspaces of V. Then W_1 \cup W_2 is a subspace of V if and only if W_1 \subseteq W_2 or W_2 \subseteq W_1. (\Leftarrow) If W_1 \subseteq W_2, then W_1 \cup W_2 = W_2, which is a subspace. Similarly, if W_2 \subseteq W_1, the union is W_1, which is also a subspace. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive: if neither is contained in the other, then the union is not a subspace. Assume W_1 
ot\subseteq W_2 and W_2 
ot\subseteq W_1. - Since W_1 
ot\subseteq W_2, there exists a vector \u \in W_1 such that \u 
otin W_2. - Since W_2 
ot\subseteq W_1, there exists a vector \v \in W_2 such that \v 
otin W_1. Consider the sum \w = \u + \v. We show that \w 
otin W_1 \cup W_2: - If \w \in W_1, then \v = \w - \u. Since \w \in W_1 and \u \in W_1, their difference \v must be in W_1 (by closure). But we chose \v 
otin W_1, which is a contradiction. - If \w \in W_2, then \u = \w - \v. Since \w \in W_2 and \v \in W_2, their difference \u must be in W_2. But we chose \u 
otin W_2, which is a contradiction. Therefore, \u + \v is in neither W_1 nor W_2, so it is not in W_1 \cup W_2. Thus, the union is not closed under addition and is therefore not a subspace.

title: 1.3 Linear Combinations and Span
content: Linear Combinations and Span In the previous section, we studied subspaces. A natural question arises: given a set of vectors, how can we describe the “smallest” subspace that contains them? This leads us to the concept of linear combinations and the span. Linear Combinations [Linear Combination] Let V be a vector space over F, S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m \} be a subset of V. Then the expression a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \cdots + a_m \v_m is called a linear combination of S. The scalars a_i are called the coefficients of the linear combination. [Examples of Linear Combinations] Below are some examples of linear combinations in different vector spaces: 1. The vector (2, 1, 0) in \nR^3 is a linear combination of S = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)\} because (2, 1, 0) = -2 \cdot (1, 2, 3) + 1 \cdot (4, 5, 6). 2. The polynomial f(x) = x^3 + 2x + 1 in \mathbb{R}[x] is a linear combination of S = \{1, x, x^2, x^3\} because f(x) = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot x + 0 \cdot x^2 + 1 \cdot x^3. Span and Spanning Sets [Span] Let S be a subset of a vector space V over F. The span of S, denoted by \Span_F(S), is the set of all linear combinations of finite subsets of elements of S. If S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \}, then \Span_F(S) = \{ a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \dots + a_n \v_n : a_i \in F \}. By convention, \Span_F(\varnothing) = \{ \mathbf{0} \}. When the underlying field is clear, we abuse the notation of \Span_F and write it as \Span. [Spanning Set as Subspace] The span of any subset S \subseteq V is a subspace of V. Moreover, it is the smallest subspace of V containing S. Let W = \Span(S). - Zero vector: Since \Span(\varnothing) = \{ \mathbf{0} \}, and for non-empty S, taking all coefficients as zero gives \mathbf{0}, we have \mathbf{0} \in W. - Addition: Let \x, \y \in W. Then \x = \sum a_i \v_i and \y = \sum b_i \v_i. Their sum \x + \y = \sum (a_i + b_i) \v_i is also a linear combination of elements in S, so \x + \y \in W. - Scalar multiplication: For any c \in F, c\x = \sum (ca_i) \v_i \in W. To see it is the smallest subspace, note that any subspace containing S must be closed under addition and scalar multiplication, and thus must contain all linear combinations of elements in S. [Spanning Set] If \Span(S) = V, we say that S spans V, or that S is a spanning set for V. [Spanning Set for Polynomials] The set \{ 1, x, x^2 \} spans \nR[x]_{\leq 2}, the space of polynomials of degree at most 2.

title: 1.4 Linear Independence
content:
Linear Independence A spanning set is like a toolbox that is guaranteed to have every tool you need. But a messy toolbox might have three different hammers that all do the same thing. In mathematics, as in engineering, we value efficiency. If one of the vectors in your spanning set can already be built using the others, then that vector is “dead weight”—it isn’t helping you reach any new territory. We call such a set linearly dependent. In this section, we search for the “cleanest” possible sets. We want to know: “Is every vector in this collection actually contributing something unique, or is someone just coasting on the work of the others?” Definition and Examples Linear Independence A subset S of a vector space V is said to be linearly independent if for any distinct vectors \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \in S, the only solution to the equation: a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \dots + a_n \v_n = \mathbf{0} is the trivial solution a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_n = 0. If there exists a non-trivial solution (where at least one a_i 
eq 0), then S is said to be linearly dependent. Geometrically, in 
R^2, two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they lie on the same line through the origin (one is a multiple of the other). In 
R^3, three vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they lie on the same plane through the origin. [Examples of Linear Independence] The following examples illustrate how to check for linear independence in various settings: 1. Let S_1 = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)\} \subseteq 
R^3. To check linear independence, suppose a(1, 2, 3) + b(4, 5, 6) = (0, 0, 0) \implies  egin{cases} a + 4b = 0 \ 2a + 5b = 0 \ 3a + 6b = 0 \end{cases} The first two equations give a = -4b and 2(-4b) + 5b = 0 \implies -3b = 0. Thus a = b = 0, so S_1 is linearly independent. 2. Let S_2 = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6), (7, 8, 9)\} \subseteq 
R^3. Note that (1, 2, 3) - 2(4, 5, 6) + (7, 8, 9) = (1-8+7, 2-10+8, 3-12+9) = (0, 0, 0). Since there exists a non-trivial solution, S_2 is linearly dependent. 3. Consider \{2x + 1, x^2 + 3\} in 
R[x]_{\leq 2}. Suppose a(2x + 1) + b(x^2 + 3) = 0 \implies bx^2 + 2ax + (a + 3b) = 0. Comparing coefficients of x^2, x, 1, we have b = 0, 2a = 0, and a + 3b = 0. This implies a = b = 0, so the set is linearly independent. 4. Consider \{ \sin x, \cos x, e^x \} in D(
R). Suppose for all x \in 
R: a \sin x + b \cos x + c e^x = 0. Setting x = 0 gives b + c = 0. Setting x = \pi gives -b + c e^\pi = 0. Adding these gives c(1 + e^\pi) = 0, so c = 0 and hence b = 0. Finally, setting x = \pi/2 gives a + c e^{\pi/2} = 0 \implies a = 0. Thus, the set is linearly independent. [Linear Dependence Lemma] \left\{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m ight\} is linearly dependent if and only if either \v_1 = \mathbf{0} or for some r, \v_r is a linear combination of \left\{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_{r - 1} ight\}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose S = \left\{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m ight\} is linearly dependent. Then there exist a_1, \dots, a_m \in F, not all zero, such that a_1 \v_1 + \cdots + a_m \v_m = \mathbf{0} . Let r be the largest index such that a_r 
eq 0. Then a_1 \v_1 + \cdots + a_{r-1} \v_{r-1} + a_r \v_r = \mathbf{0} . So a_r \v_r = -\left( a_1 \v_1 + \cdots + a_{r-1} \v_{r-1} ight), and dividing by a_r gives \v_r = - rac{a_1}{a_r}\v_1 - \cdots -  rac{a_{r-1}}{a_r}\v_{r-1}. Hence \v_r is a linear combination of \left\{ \v_1, \dots, \v_{r-1} ight\}. (If r=1, this says a_1 \v_1 = \mathbf{0} with a_1 
eq 0, so \v_1 = \mathbf{0}.) (\Leftarrow) We prove by cases: - If \v_1 = \mathbf{0}, then 1 \cdot \v_1 + 0 \cdot \v_2 + \cdots + 0 \cdot \v_m = \mathbf{0} , with coefficients not all zero, so S is linearly dependent. - If for some r we have \v_r is a linear combination of \left\{ \v_1, \dots, \v_{r-1} ight\}, then there exist scalars c_1, \dots, c_{r-1} \in F such that \v_r = c_1 \v_1 + \cdots + c_{r-1} \v_{r-1}. Move everything to one side: c_1 \v_1 + \cdots + c_{r-1} \v_{r-1} - 1 \cdot \v_r = \mathbf{0} . Extending coefficients by zeros for \v_{r+1}, \dots, \v_m, we get a nontrivial linear combination of \v_1, \dots, \v_m equal to \mathbf{0}, so S is linearly dependent. The above theorem can be paraphrased to: A set S = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \} with n \geq 2 is linearly dependent if and only if at least one vector in S can be written as a linear combination of the others. The Redundant Members Having the last remark in mind, we can develop an intuition that says linear independence of a set is equivalent to requiring the set containing no “redundant members.” Next we want to develop the intuition saying that throwing away these “redundant members” will not change the linear span. [Span Preservation] Let S = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m, \w \} \subseteq V. If \w \in \Span \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \}, then \Span(S) = \Span \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \}. Let W = \Span \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \} and W' = \Span(S). Since \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \} \subseteq S, it is clear that W \subseteq W'. For the reverse inclusion, let \v \in W'. Then \v is a linear combination of vectors in S: \v = a_1 \v_1 + \dots + a_m \v_m + b \w for some scalars a_i, b. Since \w \in W, there exist scalars c_1, \dots, c_m such that \w = c_1 \v_1 + \dots + c_m \v_m. Substituting this into the expression for \v: \v = a_1 \v_1 + \dots + a_m \v_m + b(c_1 \v_1 + \dots + c_m \v_m) = (a_1 + bc_1)\v_1 + \dots + (a_m + bc_m)\v_m. Thus \v is a linear combination of \v_1, \dots, \v_m, so \v \in W. This shows W' \subseteq W. Hence W' = W.

title: 1.5 Bases
content: Bases We have reached what many consider the “Goldilocks Zone” of Linear Algebra. If a set is too small, it won’t span the whole space—you’ll be left with points you can’t reach. If a set is too large, it will be linearly dependent—you’ll have redundant vectors cluttering your workspace. A basis is a set that is “just right.” It is large enough to build everything, but small enough that every piece is essential. Because a basis has no redundancy, it gives us something incredible: a unique address system. In an abstract vector space, it’s hard to tell someone where a vector is. But once we pick a basis, every vector can be described by a unique list of numbers—its coordinates. A basis is the bridge that allows us to turn abstract geometry into concrete arithmetic. Definition and Standard Bases [Basis] A subset B of a vector space V is called a basis for V if: 1. B is linearly independent; 2. B spans V. [Standard Bases] Commonly used standard bases for familiar vector spaces are listed below: - The standard basis for F^n is \{ \e_1, \e_2, \dots, \e_n \}, where \e_i has a 1 in the i-th position and 0 elsewhere. - The standard basis for F[x]_{\leq n} is \{ 1, x, x^2, \dots, x^n \}. - The standard basis for M_{m \times n}(F) is the set of matrices \E_{ij} having a 1 at entry (i,j) and 0 elsewhere. Unique Representation and Coordinates The most important property of a basis is that every vector in the space has a unique “address” relative to it. [Unique Representation] Let B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \} be a basis for V. Then every vector \v \in V can be written as a linear combination of elements in B in exactly one way. Since B spans V, there exist scalars a_i such that \v = \sum a_i \v_i. Suppose there is another representation \v = \sum b_i \v_i. Then: \mathbf{0} = \v - \v = \sum a_i \v_i - \sum b_i \v_i = \sum (a_i - b_i) \v_i. Since B is linearly independent, we must have a_i - b_i = 0 for all i, meaning a_i = b_i. [Coordinates] Let B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \} be an ordered basis for V. For any \v \in V, the unique scalars c_1, \dots, c_n such that \v = \sum c_i \v_i are called the coordinates of \v with respect to B. We write this as a column vector: [\v]_B = \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{bmatrix}. Notice the subtle but important distinction: a basis as a set determines which vectors can be built (i.e., it determines the space), but to define coordinates we need an ordered basis—a basis with a fixed ordering of its elements. For example, if B = \{ \v_1, \v_2 \}, then the coordinate vector [\v]_B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} means \v = 3\v_1 + 5\v_2. If we had listed the basis in the opposite order B' = \{ \v_2, \v_1 \}, the same vector \v would have coordinates [\v]_{B'} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. The underlying space is the same, but the coordinate representation depends on the ordering. The map \v \mapsto [\v]_B provides a way to treat any abstract n-dimensional vector space as if it were simply F^n. This is the power of a basis.

title: 1.6 Sifting and the Replacement Theorem
content:
Sifting and the Replacement Theorem How “big” is a vector space? We intuitively know that a plane is “bigger” than a line, and 3D space is “bigger” than a plane. But in the abstract world of vector spaces, we need a rigorous way to measure this. The answer lies in the number of vectors in a basis. But there’s a potential problem: what if one person finds a basis with 3 vectors, and another person finds a basis for the same space with 4 vectors? If that were possible, our entire concept of “size” would collapse. In this section, we prove the most important technical result of the chapter: the Steinitz Replacement Theorem. This theorem is the “engine” that guarantees every basis of a space has the exact same number of vectors. Once we have this, we can finally define the Dimension of a space—a single number that captures its fundamental complexity. The Sifting Method [Sifting Method] Let S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m \} be a subset of V. Then there exists a subset S' \subseteq S such that: 1. S' is linearly independent, and 2. \Span(S') = \Span(S). For each r = 1, 2, \dots, m, we check whether \v_r is a linear combination of the previous terms \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_{r-1}. We: 1. Keep \v_r in S' if \v_r is not a linear combination of \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_{r-1} (not redundant); 2. Remove \v_r from S' if \v_r is a linear combination of \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_{r-1} (redundant). After this process, we obtain a subset S' in which no element is a linear combination of the preceding members anymore. Therefore, by @thm-linear-dependence-lemma, S' is linearly independent. Moreover, according to @thm-span-preservation, removing “redundant members” from S does not change its linear span. Therefore, we have \Span(S') = \Span(S). The sifting method is a powerful algorithmic tool that allows us to “clean up” any set of vectors. Given any collection of vectors, we can systematically remove the redundant ones while preserving the span. This gives us a “cleaned” version that is linearly independent and spans the same space. This method becomes our “new weapon” in linear algebra proofs. Whenever we encounter a set that might have redundant vectors, we can apply the sifting method to obtain a linearly independent subset with the same span. This technique will be particularly useful in proving results about dimension and in constructing bases from spanning sets. [Sifting Example] Consider S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \v_3, \v_4, \v_5, \v_6 \} in 
R^3 where: We apply the sifting method (@thm-sift): - \v_1 
eq \mathbf{0}, so \v_1 is kept. - \v_2 = 2\v_1, so \v_2 is removed. - \v_3 is not a linear combination of \v_1, so \v_3 is kept. - \v_4 = 2\v_1 + 1\v_3, so \v_4 is removed. - Suppose \v_5 = a\v_1 + b\v_3. Then (1, 1, 0) = (a + b, a, a), which gives a = 0 and a + b = 1, so b = 1. But then the second coordinate gives 1 = a = 0, which is a contradiction. So \v_5 is not a linear combination of \v_1, \v_3. Hence, \v_5 is kept. - \v_6 = (0, 0, 1) = (1, 1, 1) - (1, 1, 0) = \v_1 - \v_5, so \v_6 is removed. The sifted set is S' = \{ \v_1, \v_3, \v_5 \} = \{ (1, 1, 1), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0) \}, which is linearly independent and spans the same space as S. [Sifting in 
R^2] Consider S = \{ (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) \} in 
R^2. - (1, 0) 
eq \mathbf{0}, so (1, 0) is kept. - (0, 1) 
otin \Span\{ (1, 0) \}, so (0, 1) is kept. - (1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1) \in \Span\{ (1, 0), (0, 1) \}, so (1, 1) is removed. The sifted set \{ (1, 0), (0, 1) \} is linearly independent and still spans 
R^2. The Steinitz Replacement Theorem [Steinitz Exchange/Replacement Theorem] Let V be a vector space over F. Suppose: - G = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \} spans V; - L = \{ \u_1, \u_2, \dots, \u_m \} is linearly independent. Then m \leq n. The strategy is to insert the vectors from L one-by-one into G and “sift” the resulting set to maintain the spanning property. We rely on the fact that if we add a vector \w to a spanning set S, the set \{ \w \} \cup S becomes linearly dependent, allowing us to remove a redundant vector (by @thm-span-preservation). Consider the first step. We form the set B_1 by inserting \u_1 into G: B_1 = \{ \u_1, \v_1, \dots, \v_n \}. Since G spans V, B_1 is linearly dependent. By applying the sifting process (@thm-sift), we can remove a vector to obtain a new spanning set G_1. Since L is linearly independent, \u_1 
eq \mathbf{0}, so the removed vector must be some \v_i. Thus: G_1 = \{ \u_1 \} \cup S_1, where S_1 is a subset of G with size n-1. Now, consider the general step. Suppose we have successfully exchanged k vectors such that the set G_k = \{ \u_1, \dots, \u_k \} \cup S_k spans V, where S_k \subset G contains n-k vectors. We insert the next vector \u_{k+1} to form: B_{k+1} = \{ \u_{k+1} \} \cup G_k. Since G_k is a spanning set, \u_{k+1} depends on the vectors in G_k, making B_{k+1} dependent. We must remove a vector to restore the spanning property. We cannot remove any of the \u_i’s, as this would imply a linear dependence relation exclusively among elements of L, contradicting the hypothesis that L is linearly independent. Therefore, we must remove some \v_j from S_k. This process generates a sequence of subsets of remaining \v’s: n = |G| > |S_1| > |S_2| > \dots > |S_m| \geq 0. Since we are able to perform this exchange m times (once for each \u \in L), we must have started with enough \v’s to accommodate every removal. Therefore, n \geq m. Consequences of the Replacement Theorem Having proved the Steinitz Replacement Theorem, the major conclusion we can draw from it is that any (finite) basis of the same vector space will have the same size. [Basis Theorem] If a vector space V over F has a finite basis, then every basis of V has the same number of vectors. Let B_1 and B_2 be two bases with n and m vectors respectively. - Since B_1 is linearly independent and B_2 spans, by Replacement Theorem, n \leq m. - Since B_2 is linearly independent and B_1 spans, by Replacement Theorem, m \leq n. Thus n = m. [Dimension] A vector space V over F is called finite-dimensional if it has a finite basis. The dimension of V, denoted \dim_F (V), is the number of vectors in any basis for V. By convention, \dim_F (\{\mathbf{0}\}) = 0. The convention \dim(\{\mathbf{0}\}) = 0 is consistent with the fact that the only basis for the zero space is the empty set \varnothing. Indeed, \varnothing is vacuously linearly independent (there is no nontrivial linear combination to consider), and \Span(\varnothing) = \{\mathbf{0}\} by our earlier convention. Since |\varnothing| = 0, we have \dim(\{\mathbf{0}\}) = 0. When the underlying field is clear, we abuse the notation of \dim_F and write it as \dim. [Examples of Dimensions] \dim(F^n) = n, \dim(F[x]_{\leq n}) = n+1, and \dim(M_{m 	imes n}(F)) = mn. The notation \dim_F(V) reminds us that dimension depends on the choice of field. For instance, recall from @exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2 that 
Q(\sqrt{2}) = \{ a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \in 
Q \} is a vector space over 
Q with basis \{ 1, \sqrt{2} \}, so \dim_{
Q}(
Q(\sqrt{2})) = 2. As a more striking example, consider the complex numbers 
C. As a vector space over itself, 
C has basis \{ 1 \}, so \dim_{
C}(
C) = 1. However, as a vector space over 
R, 
C has basis \{ 1, i \}, so \dim_{
R}(
C) = 2. The same set can have different dimensions depending on which field we use for scalar multiplication! [Size Bounds for Independent and Spanning Sets] Let V be a vector space of dimension n over F, and S \subseteq V be a subset. 1. If |S| > n, then S cannot be linearly independent. 2. If |S| < n, then S cannot span V. 1. Given |S| > n, and suppose for the sake of contradiction that S is linearly independent. Let B be a basis of V, then we have |B| = n and B is a spanning set of V. By Replacement Theorem, we have \underbrace{|S|}_{	ext{size of lin. indep. set}} \leq \underbrace{|B|}_{	ext{size of spanning set}} = n. Giving a contradiction, hence S cannot be linearly independent. 2. Given |S| < n, and suppose for the sake of contradiction that S spans V. Let B be a basis of V, then we have |B| = n and B is linearly independent. By Replacement Theorem, we have n = \underbrace{|B|}_{	ext{size of lin. indep. set}} \leq \underbrace{|S|}_{	ext{size of spanning set}}. This implies n \leq |S|, which contradicts the assumption that |S| < n. Hence S cannot span V. 	ext{Size of lin. indep. set } \leq 	ext{ Size of basis } \leq 	ext{ Size of spanning set}. [Basis Extension Theorem] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and S be a linearly independent subset of V. Then S can be extended into a basis of V. Since V is finite-dimensional, it has a finite basis B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \}. Consider the set S \cup B. Since B spans V, S \cup B also spans V. We apply the Sifting Method (@thm-sift) to the ordered set formed by listing the elements of S first, followed by the elements of B. The Sifting Method will keep all elements of S because S is linearly independent. It then proceeds to examine each element of B, keeping those that are not in the span of the vectors already kept. The resulting subset S' spans \Span(S \cup B) = V and is linearly independent by construction. Thus, S' is a basis for V that contains S. [Existence of Basis] Every finite spanning set of a vector space V contains a basis. Apply the Sifting Method (@thm-sift) to the spanning set. The resulting subset S' is linearly independent by construction and still spans V. Therefore, S' is a basis for V. [Dimension Implies Equality] Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F. If 1. W \subseteq V; 2. \dim_F (W) = \dim_F (V), then W = V. If we show V \subseteq W then we are done. Suppose for contradiction that V 
subseteq W. That means there exists some \v \in V that \v 
otin W. Let S = \{ \w_1, \dots, \w_n \} be a basis of W, (consequently, \dim_F (W) = n). Since \v 
otin W, we have \v 
otin \Span(S). Consider S' = \{ \w_1, \dots, \w_n, \v \}. Since S is linearly independent, no \w_i is a linear combination of \w_1, \dots, \w_{i-1}; and \v is not a linear combination of \w_1, \dots, \w_n because \v 
otin \Span(S). By @thm-linear-dependence-lemma, S' is linearly independent in V. By Replacement Theorem, we have \underbrace{|S'|}_{	ext{size of lin. indep. set}} \leq \dim_F (V), which implies n + 1 \leq n, which is a contradiction, therefore V \subseteq W. This theorem makes proving W = V somewhat easier. As if we wanted to prove equivalence before, we can only do it by proving W \subseteq V and V \subseteq W. Now we can just prove one side and then state that their dimension is the same. An immediate consequence of the above theorem is the following: [Maximal Independent Subset is a Basis] Let V be a vector space of dimension n over F. Then any n independent vectors form a basis of V. (We say that “any maximal linearly independent subset forms a basis”). Let S be a linearly independent set of size n. We want to show that \Span(S) = V. Let W = \Span(S), this implies that W is a subspace of V, which implies W \subseteq V. Notice that S spans W and S is linearly independent, therefore S is a basis of W. So \dim_F (W) = |S| = n = \dim_F (V). By @thm-dim-impl-eq, we have W = V, then \Span(S) = V.

title: 1.7 Sums of Subspaces
content:
Sums of Subspaces In the previous sections, we studied intersections and unions of subspaces. While the intersection of two subspaces is always a subspace, the union typically is not. This raises a natural question: what is the “right” way to combine two subspaces into a larger one? The answer is the sum of subspaces. Given two subspaces W_1 and W_2, their sum W_1 + W_2 consists of all vectors that can be written as \w_1 + \w_2 for some \w_1 \in W_1 and \w_2 \in W_2. This construction always yields a subspace—in fact, it is the smallest subspace containing both W_1 and W_2. A particularly nice situation occurs when W_1 and W_2 have only the zero vector in common. In this case, their sum is called a direct sum, and every vector in the sum can be decomposed uniquely into a piece from W_1 and a piece from W_2. Direct sums are fundamental in decomposing vector spaces into simpler, independent components. Definition and Properties [Sum of Subspaces] Let W_1, W_2 be subspaces of a vector space V. Then we define W_1 + W_2 \coloneqq \left\{ \w_1 + \w_2 : \w_1 \in W_1 	ext{ and } \w_2 \in W_2 ight\}. [Sum of Subspaces Theorem] W_1 + W_2 is a subspace of V. Furthermore, this is the smallest subspace containing both W_1 and W_2. To prove that W_1 + W_2 is a subspace of V, we verify the three conditions of the Subspace Test (@thm-subspace-test): - Non-emptiness: As W_1, W_2 are subspaces, they both contains \mathbf{0}. And since \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}_{W_1} + \mathbf{0}_{W_2}, therefore W_1 + W_2 is non-empty. - Closed under addition: Let \a,   \in W_1 + W_2. Then we have  egin{dcases} \a = \w_1 + \w_2, & 	ext{ for some } \w_1 \in W_1, \w_2 \in W_2 \   = \w_1' + \w_2', & 	ext{ for some } \w_1' \in W_1, \w_2' \in W_2 \ \end{dcases} Then \a +   = \underbrace{(\w_1 + \w_1')}_{\in W_1} + \underbrace{(\w_2 + \w_2')}_{W_2} \in W_1 + W_2. So W_1 + W_2 is closed under addition. - Closed under scalar multiplication: Let \a \in W_1 + W_2, and \lambda \in F. Then we have \a = \w_1 + \w_2 for some \w_1 \in W_1, \w_2 \in W_2. Then \lambda \a = \underbrace{\lambda \w_1}_{\in W_1} + \underbrace{\lambda \w_2}_{\in W_2} \in W_1 + W_2. So W_1 + W_2 is closed under scalar multiplication. This concludes that W_1 + W_2 is a subspace. To prove that W_1 + W_2 is the smallest subspace containing both W_1 and W_2, we first prove that it actually contains W_1 and W_2, then we prove that it is the smallest subspace of V containing so. - Containment: Since W_1 and W_2 are subspaces, they both contain the zero vector \mathbf{0}. Since for any \w_1 \in W_1, we can write \w_1 = \w_1 + \mathbf{0}, by \mathbf{0} \in W_2, we have \w_1 \in W_1 + W_2. Thus W_1 \subseteq W_1 + W_2. The same logic applies to W_2 therefore W_2 \subseteq W_1 + W_2. - Minimality: Let U be any subspace of V such that W_1 \subseteq U and W_2 \subseteq U. We want to show that W_1 + W_2 \subseteq U. Take any element W_1 + W_2. By definition \v = \w_1 + \w_2 for some \w_1 \in W_1 and \w_2 \in W_2. Because W_1 \subseteq U, then \w_1 \in U. Similarly, because W_2 \subseteq U, then \w_2 \in U. At last, since U is a subspace, it is closed under addition. Therefore \w_1 + \w_2 \in U \implies \v \in U. This concludes that W_1 + W_2 is the smallest subspace of V containing W_1 and W_2. Dimension of W_1 + W_2 [Dimension Formula of Subspace Sum] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and let W_1, W_2 subspaces of V. Then \dim(W_1 + W_2) = \dim (W_1) + \dim (W_2) - \dim(W_1 \cap W_2). We use the above diagram to build intuition for the proof. Let n = \dim(W_1 \cap W_2). Let B = \{  _1, \dots,  _n \} be a basis of the intersection W_1 \cap W_2. Since B is a linearly independent subset of both W_1 and W_2, by the Basis Extension Theorem (@thm-basis-extension), we can extend it to form bases for both subspaces: 1. For W_1: Extend B with \{ \s_1, \dots, \s_p \} such that B_1 = \{  _1, \dots,  _n, \s_1, \dots, \s_p \} is a basis of W_1. Note that \dim(W_1) = n + p. 2. For W_2: Extend B with \{ 	_1, \dots, 	_q \} such that B_2 = \{  _1, \dots,  _n, 	_1, \dots, 	_q \} is a basis of W_2. Note that \dim(W_2) = n + q. The set S = \{  _1, \dots,  _n, \s_1, \dots, \s_p, 	_1, \dots, 	_q \} is a basis of W_1 + W_2. - S spans W_1 + W_2 Let \w \in W_1 + W_2. By definition, \w = \w_1 + \w_2 for some \w_1 \in W_1, \w_2 \in W_2. Since B_1 spans W_1 and B_2 spans W_2, both \w_1 and \w_2 can be written as linear combinations of vectors in S. Thus, their sum \w is also in \Span(S). - S is Linearly Independent Consider a linear combination of vectors in S equal to the zero vector: \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i  _i + \sum_{j=1}^p  eta_j \s_j + \sum_{k=1}^q \gamma_k 	_k = \mathbf{0} {#eq-linear-combo} Rearrange the equation to isolate the terms involving 	_k: \v \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i  _i + \sum_{j=1}^p  eta_j \s_j = - \sum_{k=1}^q \gamma_k 	_k Observe the vector \v. From the LHS, we have \v \in W_1. From the RHS, we have \v \in W_2. Therefore, \v \in W_1 \cap W_2. Since \v \in W_1 \cap W_2, it can be written uniquely as a linear combination of the basis B of the intersection: \v = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i  _i Equating this with the RHS expression of \v: \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i  _i = - \sum_{k=1}^q \gamma_k 	_k \implies \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i  _i + \sum_{k=1}^q \gamma_k 	_k = \mathbf{0}. The set B_2 = \{  _1, \dots,  _n, 	_1, \dots, 	_q \} is a basis of W_2 and is therefore linearly independent. This forces all coefficients to be zero. Specifically, all \gamma_k = 0. Substitute \gamma_k = 0 back into @eq-linear-combo: \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i  _i + \sum_{j=1}^p  eta_j \s_j = \mathbf{0} Since B_1 = \{  _1, \dots,  _n, \s_1, \dots, \s_p \} is a basis of W_1, it is linearly independent. This forces all \alpha_i = 0 and all  eta_j = 0. Since all \alpha,  eta, \gamma are zero, S is linearly independent. Use dimension counting, since S is a basis for W_1 + W_2: Counter-example for 3 Subspaces It is a coincidence that this formula resembles the “Inclusion-Exclusion Principle” from set theory. This intuition fails for three or more subspaces. The formula: Counter-example: Consider three distinct lines through the origin in \mathbb{R}^2 (e.g., x-axis, y-axis, and y=x). - LHS: The sum of three lines fills the plane, so dimension is 2. - RHS: 1+1+1 - (0+0+0) + 0 = 3. Since 2 
eq 3, the formula is false. Direct Sum of Two Subspaces Direct Sum of Two Subspaces Let W_1, W_2 be subspaces of a vector space V. If W_1 \cap W_2 = \{ \mathbf{0} \}, then we write W_1 + W2 as W_1 \oplus W_2 and call it the direct sum of W_1 and W_2. Consider the vector space V = M_n (
C), and two of its subspaces: - W_1 = \{ \A \in M_n (
C) : \A^{	op} = \A \} (the subspace of symmetric matrices); - W_2 = \{ \A \in M_n (
C) : \A^{	op} = - \A \} (the subspace of skew-symmetric matrices). We can derive that V = W_1 \oplus W_2. Proof. We first show that V = W_1 + W_2. That is, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix. Let \A \in M_n (
C), notice that we have the identity: \A =  rac{1}{2} (\A + \A^{	op}) +  rac{1}{2} (\A - \A^{	op}) where the first term is symmetric and the second term is skew-symmetric. Therefore, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix. To establish that W_1 \cap W_2 = \{ \O \}, let \A \in W_1 \cap W_2. By definition, this implies \A \in W_1 and \A \in W_2. Consequently, the identities \A = \A^{	op} and \A = - \A^{	op} must hold simultaneously. Substituting the former into the latter yields \A = - \A. This implies 2\A = \O, and thus \A = \O.

title: Linear Transformations
content: Linear Transformations Vector spaces are only half of the story; the other half is the maps between them that respect addition and scalar multiplication. This chapter studies these linear transformations. Overview In this part, we will explore: - Linear transformations: the definition and basic properties, examples and non-examples, and the fact that a linear transformation is determined by its values on a basis. - Kernel and image: the two subspaces attached to every linear transformation, with examples and their basic theorems. - The rank–nullity theorem: nullity and rank, and the identity \nullity(f) + \rank(f) = \dim(V) for a finite-dimensional V.

title: 2.1 Linear Transformations
content:
Linear Transformations In Chapter 1, we studied vector spaces as static objects—sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication. Now we turn to the study of structure-preserving maps between vector spaces. Just as group theory studies homomorphisms and topology studies continuous functions, linear algebra studies linear transformations. A linear transformation is a function that “respects” the vector space structure: it preserves addition and scalar multiplication. This simple requirement has profound consequences. Linear transformations are the morphisms in the category of vector spaces, and understanding them is central to all of linear algebra. Definition and Basic Properties [Linear Transformation] Let V, W be vector spaces over F. A function T : V 	o W is called a linear transformation (or linear map), if 1. T(\v_1 + \v_2) = T(\v_1) + T(\v_2), for all \v_1, \v_2 \in V; 2. T(\lambda \v) = \lambda T(\v), for all \lambda \in F and \v \in V. Examples of Linear Transformations We now present a rich collection of examples. For each, we determine whether the given function is a linear transformation by verifying the two axioms (LT1) and (LT2). Geometric Transformations [Projection onto a Coordinate Axis] Determine whether T : 
R^2 	o 
R^2 defined by T(a_1, a_2) = (a_1, 0) is a linear transformation. Let \v = (a_1, a_2) and \w = (b_1, b_2) be vectors in 
R^2, and let \lambda \in 
R. - Additivity: T(\v + \w) = T(a_1 + b_1, a_2 + b_2) = (a_1 + b_1, 0) = (a_1, 0) + (b_1, 0) = T(\v) + T(\w). - Homogeneity: T(\lambda \v) = T(\lambda a_1, \lambda a_2) = (\lambda a_1, 0) = \lambda (a_1, 0) = \lambda T(\v). Thus T is a linear transformation. [Rotation in the Plane] Determine whether rotation by angle 	heta (counterclockwise) in the plane is a linear transformation. That is, let T_	heta : 
R^2 	o 
R^2 be the rotation map. Write (a_1, a_2) in polar coordinates: a_1 = r\cos\phi and a_2 = r\sin\phi. Then: Thus T_	heta(a_1, a_2) = (a_1\cos	heta - a_2\sin	heta, \; a_1\sin	heta + a_2\cos	heta). Linearity follows from this explicit formula: for \v, \w \in 
R^2 and \lambda \in 
R, where J(a_1, a_2) = (-a_2, a_1) is itself linear. Matrix-Induced Transformations [Left Multiplication by a Matrix] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) be an m 	imes n matrix. Determine whether f_\A : F^n 	o F^m defined by f_\A(\v) = \A\v (where \v is viewed as a column vector) is a linear transformation. For \v, \w \in F^n and \lambda \in F: - Additivity: f_\A(\v + \w) = \A(\v + \w) = \A\v + \A\w = f_\A(\v) + f_\A(\w). - Homogeneity: f_\A(\lambda\v) = \A(\lambda\v) = \lambda(\A\v) = \lambda f_\A(\v). These follow from the distributive and scalar properties of matrix multiplication (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties). For F = 
R and m = n = 2, the map f_\A sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by \A\e_1 and \A\e_2, the columns of \A. The unit square (dashed) and its image under \A =  egin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Drag the tips of the two arrows to change \A. [A Specific Matrix Transformation] Determine whether T : F^3 	o F^2 defined by T(a_1, a_2, a_3) = (2a_1 + a_3, \; a_2 - a_1) is a linear transformation. This is the matrix transformation induced by \A =  egin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, since  egin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}  egin{bmatrix} a_1 \ a_2 \ a_3 \end{bmatrix} =  egin{bmatrix} 2a_1 + a_3 \ a_2 - a_1 \end{bmatrix}. By the previous example, T is linear. [Trace] Determine whether the trace function 	r : M_n(F) 	o F defined by 	r(\A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ii} is a linear transformation. For matrices \A, \B \in M_n(F) and \lambda \in F: - Additivity: 	r(\A + \B) = \sum_{i=1}^n (a_{ii} + b_{ii}) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ii} + \sum_{i=1}^n b_{ii} = 	r(\A) + 	r(\B). - Homogeneity: 	r(\lambda\A) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda a_{ii} = \lambda \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ii} = \lambda	r(\A). Thus trace is a linear transformation from the vector space of matrices to the scalar field. Polynomial and Function Space Transformations [Multiplication by x] Determine whether T : F[x] 	o F[x] defined by T(f(x)) = x \cdot f(x) is a linear transformation. For polynomials f, g \in F[x] and \lambda \in F: - Additivity: T(f + g) = x(f + g) = xf + xg = T(f) + T(g). - Homogeneity: T(\lambda f) = x(\lambda f) = \lambda(xf) = \lambda T(f). Thus multiplication by x is a linear transformation. [Differentiation] Determine whether D : 
R[x] 	o 
R[x] defined by D(f(x)) = f'(x) (the derivative) is a linear transformation. For polynomials f, g \in 
R[x] and \lambda \in 
R: - Additivity: D(f + g) = (f + g)' = f' + g' = D(f) + D(g). - Homogeneity: D(\lambda f) = (\lambda f)' = \lambda f' = \lambda D(f). These are the standard sum rule and constant multiple rule from calculus. More precisely, D : 
R[x]_{\leq n} 	o 
R[x]_{\leq n-1} maps polynomials of degree at most n to polynomials of degree at most n-1. [Integration] Determine whether T : 
R[x] 	o 
R[x] defined by T(f(x)) = \int_0^x f(t) \, \dd t is a linear transformation. For polynomials f, g \in 
R[x] and \lambda \in 
R: - Additivity: T(f + g) = \int_0^x (f(t) + g(t)) \, \dd t = \int_0^x f(t) \, \dd t + \int_0^x g(t) \, \dd t = T(f) + T(g). - Homogeneity: T(\lambda f) = \int_0^x \lambda f(t) \, \dd t = \lambda \int_0^x f(t) \, \dd t = \lambda T(f). These follow from the linearity of the integral. [Shift Operator] Fix 	heta \in 
R. Determine whether the shift operator S_	heta : C(
R) 	o C(
R) defined by S_	heta(f)(x) = f(x - 	heta) is a linear transformation. (This operator translates the graph of f by 	heta units to the right.) For f, g \in C(
R) and \lambda \in 
R: - Additivity: S_	heta(f + g)(x) = (f + g)(x - 	heta) = f(x - 	heta) + g(x - 	heta) = S_	heta(f)(x) + S_	heta(g)(x). - Homogeneity: S_	heta(\lambda f)(x) = (\lambda f)(x - 	heta) = \lambda f(x - 	heta) = \lambda S_	heta(f)(x). Thus the shift operator is linear. [Composition Operator] Fix a continuous function g : 
R 	o 
R. Determine whether the composition operator C_g : C(
R) 	o C(
R) defined by C_g(f) = f \circ g, i.e., C_g(f)(x) = f(g(x)), is a linear transformation. For f, h \in C(
R) and \lambda \in 
R: - Additivity: C_g(f + h)(x) = (f + h)(g(x)) = f(g(x)) + h(g(x)) = C_g(f)(x) + C_g(h)(x). - Homogeneity: C_g(\lambda f)(x) = (\lambda f)(g(x)) = \lambda f(g(x)) = \lambda C_g(f)(x). The shift operator is the special case where g(x) = x - 	heta. Identity and Inclusion Maps [Identity Map] Let V be a vector space. Determine whether the identity map \id_V : V 	o V defined by \id_V(\v) = \v is a linear transformation. For \v, \w \in V and \lambda \in F: - Additivity: \id_V(\v + \w) = \v + \w = \id_V(\v) + \id_V(\w). - Homogeneity: \id_V(\lambda\v) = \lambda\v = \lambda\id_V(\v). The identity map is trivially linear. [Inclusion Map] Let W \subseteq V be a subspace. Determine whether the inclusion map \iota : W \hookrightarrow V defined by \iota(\w) = \w is a linear transformation. The inclusion map is simply the identity map restricted to W, viewed as a map into V. The verification is identical to the identity map. [Zero Map] For any vector spaces V and W, determine whether the zero map 0 : V 	o W defined by 0(\v) = \mathbf{0}_W for all \v \in V is a linear transformation. For \v_1, \v_2 \in V and \lambda \in F: - Additivity: 0(\v_1 + \v_2) = \mathbf{0}_W = \mathbf{0}_W + \mathbf{0}_W = 0(\v_1) + 0(\v_2). - Homogeneity: 0(\lambda\v_1) = \mathbf{0}_W = \lambda\mathbf{0}_W = \lambda \cdot 0(\v_1). The zero map is linear. Field-Dependent Examples [Complex Conjugation] Determine whether complex conjugation T : 
C 	o 
C defined by T(z) = \overline{z}, where \overline{a + bi} = a - bi, is a linear transformation. As a map of 
C-vector spaces: T is not linear over 
C. Consider z = 1 and \alpha = i. Then: T(\alpha z) = T(i) = -i, \quad 	ext{but} \quad \alpha T(z) = i \cdot \overline{1} = i. Since T(i \cdot 1) = -i 
eq i = i \cdot T(1), the homogeneity condition fails. As a map of 
R-vector spaces: T is linear over 
R. For z = a + bi and w = c + di with a, b, c, d \in 
R, and \lambda \in 
R: - Additivity: T(z + w) = \overline{(a+c) + (b+d)i} = (a+c) - (b+d)i = (a - bi) + (c - di) = T(z) + T(w). - Homogeneity: T(\lambda z) = \overline{\lambda a + \lambda bi} = \lambda a - \lambda bi = \lambda(a - bi) = \lambda T(z). This example illustrates that linearity depends on the choice of scalar field. Non-Examples of Linear Transformations It is equally important to recognize functions that are not linear transformations. We verify non-linearity by finding a counterexample to either (LT1) or (LT2). [Squaring] Determine whether T : F^2 	o F^2 defined by T(a_1, a_2) = (a_1^2, 0) is a linear transformation. We show that T fails additivity. Consider \v = (1, 0): T(\v) + T(\v) = (1, 0) + (1, 0) = (2, 0), but T(\v + \v) = T(2, 0) = (4, 0). Since (2, 0) 
eq (4, 0), additivity fails and T is not linear. Alternatively, homogeneity fails: T(2\v) = T(2, 0) = (4, 0) 
eq 2 \cdot (1, 0) = (2, 0) = 2T(\v). [Norm] Determine whether T : 
R^n 	o 
R defined by T(\v) = \|\v\| (the Euclidean norm) is a linear transformation. Homogeneity fails for negative scalars. Consider \v = (1, 0, \ldots, 0) and \lambda = -1: T(\lambda\v) = T(-1, 0, \ldots, 0) = \|(-1, 0, \ldots, 0)\| = 1, but \lambda T(\v) = (-1) \cdot \|(1, 0, \ldots, 0)\| = -1. Since 1 
eq -1, homogeneity fails and T is not a linear transformation. (The norm does satisfy \|c\v\| = |c| \|\v\|, but this is not the same as c\|\v\| when c < 0.) Basic Theorems [Zero Maps to Zero] Let T: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Then T(\mathbf{0}_V) = \mathbf{0}_W. Using additivity with \v = \mathbf{0}_V: T(\mathbf{0}_V) = T(\mathbf{0}_V + \mathbf{0}_V) = T(\mathbf{0}_V) + T(\mathbf{0}_V). Adding -T(\mathbf{0}_V) to both sides gives \mathbf{0}_W = T(\mathbf{0}_V). This theorem provides a quick test for non-linearity: if T(\mathbf{0}) 
eq \mathbf{0}, then T is not linear. [Constant Function] Determine whether T : 
R 	o 
R defined by T(x) = 5 for all x \in 
R is a linear transformation. We use @thm-zero-maps-to-zero: any linear transformation must map zero to zero. Here, T(0) = 5 
eq 0. Therefore, T is not a linear transformation. [Translation] Determine whether T : 
R^2 	o 
R^2 defined by T(\v) = \v + \mathbf{c} for some fixed nonzero \mathbf{c} \in 
R^2 is a linear transformation. Using @thm-zero-maps-to-zero: T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} 
eq \mathbf{0}. Therefore, translation by a nonzero vector is not linear. Maps of the form \v \mapsto \A\v + \mathbf{c} are called affine transformations. They are linear if and only if \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}. [Linear Maps Preserve Negation] Let T: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Then T(-\v) = -T(\v) for all \v \in V. Using homogeneity with \lambda = -1: T(-\v) = T((-1)\v) = (-1)T(\v) = -T(\v). [Equivalent Characterization of Linearity] Let V, W be vector spaces over F and T: V 	o W be a function. Then T is a linear transformation if and only if T(\alpha \v_1 +  eta \v_2) = \alpha T(\v_1) +  eta T(\v_2) for all \alpha,  eta \in F and \v_1, \v_2 \in V. (\Rightarrow) Suppose T is linear. Then for any \alpha,  eta \in F and \v_1, \v_2 \in V: (\Leftarrow) Suppose T(\alpha \v_1 +  eta \v_2) = \alpha T(\v_1) +  eta T(\v_2) for all \alpha,  eta \in F and \v_1, \v_2 \in V. - Additivity (LT1): Setting \alpha =  eta = 1, we get T(\v_1 + \v_2) = T(\v_1) + T(\v_2). - Homogeneity (LT2): Setting  eta = 0, we get T(\alpha \v_1 + \mathbf{0}) = \alpha T(\v_1) + 0 \cdot T(\v_2), i.e., T(\alpha \v_1) = \alpha T(\v_1). Thus T satisfies both (LT1) and (LT2), so T is linear. [Linear Maps Preserve Linear Combinations] Let T: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Then for any vectors \v_1, \ldots, \v_n \in V and scalars a_1, \ldots, a_n \in F: T\left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i \v_i ight) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i T(\v_i). By induction on n. The base case n = 1 is homogeneity. For the inductive step: Linear Transformation Determined by Basis Another useful fact of a linear transformation is that once we know how it acts on a basis, then we know how it acts on every vector in the domain. [Linear Transformations are Determined by Their Action on a Basis] Let T: V 	o W be a linear transformation and V is finite dimensional, and B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \} be a basis for V. Then we have: 1. For every \v \in V, f(\v) is a linear combination of f(\v_1), f(\v_2), \dots, f(\v_n). 2. Suppose the linear transformation g : V 	o W satisfies g(\v_i) = f(\v_i) for all i. Then g = f. We say ‘f is determined by f(\v_1), \dots, f(\v_n)’ in this case. Let \v \in V. Since B is a basis of V, we can write \v = \alpha_1 \v_1 + \dots + \alpha_n \v_n. Then This proves the first condition. Moreover, if g : V 	o W satisfies g(\v_i) = f(\v_i), then: Since g(\v) = f(\v) for all \v \in V, we have f = g. This finishes the second condition. title: 2.2 Kernel and Image
content:
Kernel and Image Definition [Kernel] Let f: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Define the kernel of f by \ker (f) \coloneqq \left\{ \v \in V : f(\v) = \mathbf{0}_W ight\}. i.e. The kernel contains everything in the domain that becomes the zero vector under f. [Image] Let f: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Define the image of f by \im (f) \coloneqq \left\{ \w \in W : \w = f(\v) 	ext{ for some } \v \in V ight\}. i.e. The image contains all the possible outputs of the function f. The kernel is also known as the nullspace, which you might be familiar from Gilbert Strang’s book. And the image is also called the range. Also, we sometimes denote the image as f(V). Examples [Differentiation] Let D : 
R[x]_{\leq 3} 	o 
R[x]_{\leq 2} be defined by D(f(x)) = f'(x). Find the kernel and image of D. Kernel: We seek all polynomials f(x) \in 
R[x]_{\leq 3} such that D(f(x)) = f'(x) = 0. A polynomial has derivative zero if and only if it is a constant. Thus: \ker(D) = \{ c : c \in 
R \} = \Span\{1\}. So \dim(\ker(D)) = 1. Image: We need to determine which polynomials in 
R[x]_{\leq 2} can be obtained as derivatives. Let f(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + a_3 x^3 \in 
R[x]_{\leq 3}. Then: D(f(x)) = f'(x) = a_1 + 2a_2 x + 3a_3 x^2. As a_1, a_2, a_3 range over all real numbers, we can obtain any polynomial of degree at most 2. Therefore: \im(D) = 
R[x]_{\leq 2}. So \dim(\im(D)) = 3. Note that \dim(\ker(D)) + \dim(\im(D)) = 1 + 3 = 4 = \dim(
R[x]_{\leq 3}). [Trace] Let 	r : M_2(
R) 	o 
R be defined by 	r(\A) = a_{11} + a_{22}. Find the kernel and image of 	r. Kernel: We seek all matrices \A \in M_2(
R) such that 	r(\A) = 0. Let \A =  egin{bmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{bmatrix}. Then 	r(\A) = a + d = 0, which means d = -a. So the kernel consists of all matrices of the form: \A =  egin{bmatrix} a & b \ c & -a \end{bmatrix} = a egin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + b egin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + c egin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. Therefore: \ker(	r) = \Span\left\{  egin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix},  egin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},  egin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ight\}. So \dim(\ker(	r)) = 3. Image: For any r \in 
R, we can find a matrix with trace r, for example  egin{bmatrix} r & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. Therefore: \im(	r) =

R)). Basic Theorems [Properties of Kernel] Let f: V 	o W be a linear transformation. Then: 1. \im (f) is a subspace of W; 2. f is surjective iff \im (f) = W. 1. - Non-emptiness: Since f is linear, \mathbf{0}_W = f(\mathbf{0}_V), therefore \mathbf{0}_W \in \im (f). - Closure under addition: Let \w_1, \w_2 \in im (f). So \w_1 = f(\v_1), and \w_2 = f(\v_2) for some \v_1, \v_2 \in V. Notice that \w_1 + \w_2 = f(\v_1) + f(\v_2) = f(\v_1 + \v_2). Therefore \w_1 + \w_2 \in \im (f). - Closure under scalar multiplication: Let \w \in \im (f). So \w =  (\v) for some \v \in V. Notice that \lambda \w = \lambda f(\v) = f(\lambda \v). Therefore \lambda \w \in \im (f). 2. f is surjective \Leftrightarrow  orall\w \in W, we have \w \in f(\v) for some \v \in V, that is equivalent to say W \subseteq \im (f), and by the first condition we know that \im (f) \subseteq W is always true. Hence we have f is surjective \Leftrightarrow W = \im (f).

title: Definition 0.1.1 (Negation, conjunction, disjunction)
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. The negation \(\neg P\) (“not \(P\) ”) is true when \(P\) is false, and false when \(P\) is true. The conjunction \(P \wedge Q\) (“ \(P\) and \(Q\) ”) is true when both \(P\) and \(Q\) are true, and false otherwise. The disjunction \(P \vee Q\) (“ \(P\) or \(Q\) ”) is true when at least one of \(P\) , \(Q\) is true, and false only when both are false.

title: Definition 0.1.2 (Implication, converse, contrapositive)
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. The implication \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (“if \(P\) then \(Q\) ”) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false, and it is true in every other case. We call \(P\) the hypothesis and \(Q\) the conclusion . The converse of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is the implication \(Q \Rightarrow P\) . The contrapositive of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is the implication \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) .

title: Definition 0.1.4 (Negation of quantifiers)
content:
Let \(P(x)\) be a predicate with \(x\) ranging over \(S\) . Then \[ 
eg igl( orall x \in S : P(x) igr) \ \equiv\ \exists x \in S : 
eg P(x), \qquad 
eg igl(\exists x \in S : P(x) igr) \ \equiv\  orall x \in S : 
eg P(x). \] For a statement with several quantifiers, apply these rules from the outside in: each \( orall\) becomes \(\exists\) , each \(\exists\) becomes \( orall\) , the ranges stay the same, and the innermost condition is negated using @thm-de-morgan-logic .

title: Definition 0.1.3 (Quantifiers)
content: Let \(P(x)\) be a predicate whose variable \(x\) ranges over a fixed collection \(S\) . The universal statement \(\forall x \in S : P(x)\) (“for every \(x\) in \(S\) , \(P(x)\) ”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for every element \(x\) of \(S\) , and false otherwise. The existential statement \(\exists x \in S : P(x)\) (“there exists \(x\) in \(S\) such that \(P(x)\) ”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for at least one element \(x\) of \(S\) , and false otherwise. The symbols \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) are the universal and existential quantifiers .

title: Example (What “not injective” means)
content: A function \(f\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is called injective if \[ \forall a_1 \in A \ \forall a_2 \in A : \bigl( f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2 \bigr). \] Write down, with no “not” in front, what it means for \(f\) to be not injective. content: Consider the pairs \((1, 2)\) , \((2, 4)\) , \((0, 1)\) , and the statement \[ \forall a, b, c \in \nR : \Bigl( a(1, 2) + b(2, 4) + c(0, 1) = (0, 0) \ \Rightarrow\ a = 0 \wedge b = 0 \wedge c = 0 \Bigr). \] Negate it, and decide which of the statement and its negation is true.

title: Exercise (C1: Exporting a hypothesis)
content: Prove that \(P \Rightarrow (Q \Rightarrow R)\) is logically equivalent to \((P \wedge Q) \Rightarrow R\) for all statements \(P, Q, R\) . Explain in one sentence why this lets a theorem with two hypotheses be stated either way.

title: Exercise (C2: When can a converse fail too?)

Explain why (a) and (b) do not contradict each other.

title: Theorem 0.1.1 (Contrapositive equivalence)
content: For all statements \(P\) and \(Q\) , the implication \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) .

title: Definition 0.2.2 (Divisibility and primes)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers. We say \(a\) divides \(b\) , written \(a \mid b\) , if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(b = ak\) . An integer \(p\) is prime if \(p \ge 2\) and the only positive divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\) .

title: Definition 0.2.1 (Even and odd)
content: An integer \(n\) is even if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k\) . An integer \(n\) is odd if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k + 1\) .

title: Example (Refuting “every prime is odd”)
content: Decide whether every prime number is odd. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For each statement, name the proof technique you would use first (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, induction, or counterexample), and give a one-sentence reason. Then carry out the proof or refutation. The sum of two odd integers is even. For every integer \(n\) , if \(3n + 2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd. For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \(3 \mid 4^n - 1\) . For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \(n^2 \ge 2n\) . There is no largest integer.

title: Exercise (B1: Contrapositive)
content: Prove that for every integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd.

title: Exercise (B2: Induction)
content: Prove that for every integer \(n \ge 1\) , the sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is \(n^2\) : \[ 1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n - 1) = n^2. \]

title: Exercise (B3: \sqrt{3} is irrational)
content: You may use the school fact that every integer has exactly one of the forms \(3k\) , \(3k + 1\) , \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer. Prove that for every integer \(n\) , if \(3 \mid n^2\) then \(3 \mid n\) . Hence prove that there is no rational number whose square is \(3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Stamps of 4 and 5)
content: Show that each of \(12, 13, 14, 15\) can be written as \(4a + 5b\) with \(a, b \in \nN\) . Prove by strong induction that every integer \(n \ge 12\) can be written as \(4a + 5b\) with \(a, b \in \nN\) . Show that \(11\) cannot be written in this form, so the bound \(12\) in (b) cannot be lowered to \(11\) . Hint: for \(n \ge 16\) , look at \(n - 4\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Division with remainder)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers with \(b \ge 1\) . Let \(R\) be the collection of all non-negative integers of the form \(a - qb\) with \(q\) an integer. Show that \(R\) is non-empty. Let \(r\) be the least element of \(R\) , which exists by @thm-well-ordering , and write \(r = a - qb\) . Prove that \(0 \le r < b\) . Prove that the pair \((q, r)\) is unique: if \(a = qb + r = q'b + r'\) with \(0 \le r < b\) and \(0 \le r' < b\) , then \(q = q'\) and \(r = r'\) . Hint for (a): try \(q = -\lvert a \rvert\) .

title: Proposition 0.2.5 (Parity of a square)
content: For every integer \(n\) , \(n\) is even if and only if \(n^2\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.6 (Uniqueness of the identity)
content: Let \(\ast\) be a binary operation on \(S\) . Then \(\ast\) has at most one identity element.

title: Proposition 0.2.4 (n^2 + n is even)
content: For every integer \(n\) , the integer \(n^2 + n\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.9 (2^n > n)
content: For every natural number \(n\) , we have \(2^n > n\) .

title: Proposition 0.2.12 (Existence of a prime factor)
content: Every integer \(n \ge 2\) has a prime divisor.

title: Proposition 0.2.2 (Even squares)
content: For every integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.8 (Sum of the first n integers)
content: For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \[ 1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. \]

title: Proposition 0.2.1 (Sum of even integers)
content: For all integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are even, then \(m + n\) is even.

title: Theorem 0.2.7 (Principle of Mathematical Induction)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose ( base case ) \(P(n_0)\) is true, and ( inductive step ) for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , if \(P(n)\) is true then \(P(n + 1)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 0.2.13 (Infinitely many primes)
content: There are infinitely many prime numbers.

title: Theorem 0.2.3 (Irrationality of \sqrt{2})
content: There is no rational number whose square is \(2\) . That is, \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

title: Theorem 0.2.10 (Strong induction)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose that for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , \[ \text{if } P(k) \text{ is true for all integers } k \text{ with } n_0 \le k < n, \text{ then } P(n) \text{ is true.} \] Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 0.2.11 (Well-Ordering Principle)
content: Every non-empty collection of natural numbers has a least element: an element \(m\) of the collection with \(m \le s\) for every \(s\) in the collection.

title: Definition 0.3.10 (Cartesian product)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. The Cartesian product of \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of ordered pairs \[ A \times B = \{ (a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \}. \] More generally, for sets \(A_1, \dots, A_n\) , the product \(A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n\) is the set of all ordered lists \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with \(a_i \in A_i\) for each \(i\) .

title: Definition 0.3.1 (Common number sets)
content:
We write \(
N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}\) for the natural numbers ; in this book \(
N\) includes \(0\) ; \(
Z = \{\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) for the integers ; \(
Q\) for the rational numbers , the numbers \(a/b\) with \(a, b \in 
Z\) and \(b 
e 0\) ; \(
R\) for the real numbers ; \(
C\) for the complex numbers , studied later in this chapter.

title: Definition 0.3.3 (Empty set)
content: The empty set \(\varnothing\) is the set with no elements: \(x \notin \varnothing\) for every object \(x\) .

title: Definition 0.3.9 (Unions and intersections of indexed families)
content: Let \(I\) be a set, and for each \(i \in I\) let \(A_i\) be a set. The collection \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) is an indexed family of sets, with index set \(I\) . Its union is \[ \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \{ x : \exists i \in I : x \in A_i \}, \] and, if \(I\) is non-empty , its intersection is \[ \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \{ x : \forall i \in I : x \in A_i \}. \]

title: Definition 0.3.7 (Intersection)
content: The intersection of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \cap B = \{ x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B \}. \] We call \(A\) and \(B\) disjoint if \(A \cap B = \varnothing\) .

title: Definition 0.3.11 (n-tuples)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(n \ge 1\) an integer. An \(n\) -tuple of elements of \(A\) is an ordered list \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with each \(a_i \in A\) . The set of all of them is \[ A^n = \underbrace{A \times A \times \cdots \times A}_{n \text{ factors}}. \] Two \(n\) -tuples are equal exactly when \(a_i = b_i\) for every \(i = 1, \dots, n\) .

title: Definition 0.3.12 (Power set)
content: The power set of a set \(S\) is the set of all subsets of \(S\) : \[ \powerset{S} = \{ X : X \subseteq S \}. \]

title: Definition 0.3.2 (Set-builder notation)
content: Let \(S\) be a set and let \(P(x)\) be a predicate for \(x \in S\) . The set \[ \{ x \in S : P(x) \} \] is the set whose elements are exactly those \(x \in S\) for which \(P(x)\) is true.

title: Definition 0.3.8 (Set difference and complement)
content: The difference of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \setminus B = \{ x \in A : x \notin B \}. \] When all sets under discussion are subsets of one fixed set \(U\) , the complement of \(B \subseteq U\) is \(B^{c} = U \setminus B\) .

title: Definition 0.3.5 (Set equality)
content: Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are equal , written \(A = B\) , if they have exactly the same elements: \[ \forall x : \bigl( x \in A \Leftrightarrow x \in B \bigr). \]

title: Definition 0.3.4 (Subset)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We say \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) , and write \(A \subseteq B\) , if \[ \forall x : \bigl( x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B \bigr). \] If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(A \ne B\) , then \(A\) is a proper subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subsetneq B\) .

title: Definition 0.3.6 (Union)
content: The union of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \cup B = \{ x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B \}. \]

title: Example (Indexed unions and intersections of intervals)
content: For each integer \(n \ge 1\) , let \(A_n = [1/n, 1]\) and \(B_n = (0, 1/n)\) . Show that \[ \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n = (0, 1] \qquad \text{and} \qquad \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n = \varnothing. \] You may use the fact that for every real \(x > 0\) there is an integer \(n \ge 1\) with \(1/n < x\) .

Give a one-line reason. \(0 \in \nN\) . \(\varnothing \in \varnothing\) . \(\varnothing \subseteq \varnothing\) . \(\{0\} = \varnothing\) . \(\{1, 2\} = \{2, 1, 1\}\) and \((1, 2) = (2, 1)\) . \(\{1\} \in \powerset{\{1, 2\}}\) and \(\{1\} \subseteq \powerset{\{1, 2\}}\) .

title: Exercise (B1: The second De Morgan law)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) be sets. Prove that \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) , which is part (b) of @thm-de-morgan-sets .

title: Exercise (B2: A distributive law)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) , which is part (a) of @thm-distributive-sets .

title: Exercise (B3: An indexed intersection)
content: Prove that \[ \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \Bigl( -\frac1n, \frac1n \Bigr) = \{0\}. \] You may use the fact that for every real \(x > 0\) there is an integer \(n \ge 1\) with \(1/n < x\) .

title: Exercise (C1: When union equals intersection)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cup B = A \cap B\) if and only if \(A = B\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Counting subsets)
content: For a finite set \(S\) , write \(\lvert S \rvert\) for its number of elements. The aim is to prove that \(\lvert \powerset{S} \rvert = 2^{\lvert S \rvert}\) for every finite set \(S\) . Check the claim when \(S = \varnothing\) . Let \(S\) have \(n + 1\) elements, fix \(s \in S\) , and let \(S' = S \setminus \{s\}\) . Show that every subset \(X\) of \(S\) belongs to exactly one of the two collections: the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \notin X\) , and the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \in X\) . Show that the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \notin X\) are exactly the subsets of \(S'\) , and that \(X \mapsto X \setminus \{s\}\) and \(T \mapsto T \cup \{s\}\) pair off the subsets of \(S\) containing \(s\) with the subsets of \(S'\) , each undoing the other. Hence prove the claim by induction on \(n = \lvert S \rvert\) . Hint: in (c), use double inclusion to check that \((X \setminus \{s\}) \cup \{s\} = X\) when \(s \in X\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.2 (De Morgan’s laws for sets)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. Then \(A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)\) ; \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) . In particular, if \(B, C \subseteq U\) , then \((B \cup C)^{c} = B^{c} \cap C^{c}\) and \((B \cap C)^{c} = B^{c} \cup C^{c}\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.3 (Distributive laws for sets)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. Then \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) ; \(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.1 (Double inclusion)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Definition 0.4.4 (Composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. The composition \(g \circ f \colon X \to Z\) is defined by \[ (g \circ f)(x) \coloneqq g\big(f(x)\big) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X. \]

title: Definition 0.4.1 (Function)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A function (or map ) \(f \colon X \to Y\) is a rule that assigns to every element \(x \in X\) exactly one element \(f(x) \in Y\) . The set \(X\) is the domain of \(f\) , the set \(Y\) is its codomain , and \(f(x)\) is the value of \(f\) at \(x\) . We also write \(x \mapsto f(x)\) . Two functions \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon X' \to Y'\) are equal if \(X = X'\) , \(Y = Y'\) , and \(f(x) = g(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) .

title: Definition 0.4.5 (Identity function)
content: For a set \(X\) , the identity function on \(X\) is \(\id_X \colon X \to X\) , \(\id_X(x) = x\) .

title: Definition 0.4.2 (Image and preimage)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, \(A \subseteq X\) and \(B \subseteq Y\) . The image of \(A\) under \(f\) is \(f(A) \coloneqq \{ f(a) : a \in A \} \subseteq Y\) . The set \(f(X)\) is called the image of \(f\) . The preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) is \(f^{-1}(B) \coloneqq \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \} \subseteq X\) .

title: Definition 0.4.3 (Injective, surjective, bijective)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. \(f\) is injective (one-to-one) if for all \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) , \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) . \(f\) is surjective (onto) if for every \(y \in Y\) there exists \(x \in X\) with \(f(x) = y\) . Equivalently, \(f(X) = Y\) . \(f\) is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

title: Definition 0.4.7 (Inverse function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is an inverse of \(f\) if \[ g \circ f = \id_X \qquad \text{and} \qquad f \circ g = \id_Y. \] If \(f\) has an inverse, \(f\) is invertible .

title: Definition 0.4.6 (Left and right inverses)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a left inverse of \(f\) if \(g \circ f = \id_X\) , and a right inverse of \(f\) if \(f \circ g = \id_Y\) .
